newsitem.title: USA: NYS PROBES EUROPE INSURERS OVER HOLOCAUST VICTIMS.
newsitem.headline: NYS PROBES EUROPE INSURERS OVER HOLOCAUST VICTIMS.

text.p: New York State Governor George Pataki Wednesday said he was expanding efforts to help Holocaust victims by launching a probe into European insurers and what he called their failure to compensate the victims.

Pataki said the state insurance department will start by identifying insurance companies that wrote policies throughout Europe from 1993 to 1945. By early September, the state Superintendent of Insurance will meet the chief executive officers of the companies.
"Those who experienced the atrocities of the Holocaust and who once were powerless as the world stood by and watched, no longer stand alone," Pataki said, in prepared remarks.

Asked whether Albany was the first to examine how European insurance companies treated the Holocaust victims, Charles Deister, a spokesman for Pataki said: "New York is at the forefront on this issue."
New York City is an international banking center.

The furor over how Swiss banks handled accounts left by Jews and others killed by Nazis has hurt Switzerland's image abroad from the past two years, according to opinion polls. A "solidarity foundation," with capital of around seven billion Swiss francs ($4.6 billion), is supposed to help charities at home and abroad as a way of repairing the country's image.

Swiss banks in late July took an unprecedented step to appease their critics by breaking traditional secrecy to publish the names of more than 1,870 foreigners who opened Swiss accounts before the end of World War Two in 1945.

The New York State governor in May set up a Commission on the Recovery of Holocaust Victims' Assets, stepping up Albany's efforts to identify unclaimed assets of Holocaust victims that might have been deposited in Swiss bank accounts. Later this month, a Holocaust Claims Processing Office, which will be part of the state banking department, will be opened in Manhattan to help the victims and their families file claims against Swiss banks.
